title: Christ overturns the unlawful doctrine of souls sent into bodies
english: In this, the Savior himself was overturning an unlawful doctrine. For some people supposed that sinning souls are sent from heaven into a body for the sake of punishment, and that sometimes the soul remains pre-existing by itself apart from the body, while at other times it is intertwined with bodies on account of its own sins—so that a woman can conceive only when some soul sins. Destroying this error, Christ, when he was asked, said: "Neither this man sinned nor his parents, but this happened so that the works of God might be revealed" (John 3).
translator_notes: The source text is a fragment; the Greek begins mid-sentence ('Ἐν τούτῳ δὲ...') and ends mid-sentence ('...ἔργα θεοῦ'). The final clause 'ἵνα φανερωθῇ τὰ ἔργα θεοῦ' is a complete sentence in itself, but the preceding text is a run-on sentence in Greek. The translation reflects the Greek structure as closely as possible while maintaining English grammar.
The phrase 'τότε κατὰ γαστρὸς ἔχειν τὴν γυναῖκα' is translated literally as 'then to be able to have the woman in the belly', referring to the act of procreation or sexual intercourse.

The Greek text contains a gap: 'τοῦ σώματος <μένειν>'. The angle brackets indicate a missing word or words. The translation assumes the missing word is a verb or participle related to remaining or abiding, as the context suggests the soul's relationship to the body.
baehrens: PG 65; Fragmenta in Joannem (Khazarzar) u01 open
orientation: The author introduces a fragment on John 3, explaining that Christ himself overturned an unlawful doctrine held by some about souls being sent into bodies for punishment.
